Hunt Training
        Some horses, especially coursers, are trained for the hunt.
      When required to make a Horsemanship roll while hunting or
      otherwise chasing something through the woods, add a +5 mod-
      ifier to your skill while riding a trained hunting steed.
      Combat Training

        Horses can be trained for combat, and must be if the rider
      is to concentrate fully on his task. All horses labeled Charger,
      Courser, Rouncy, and Destrier are assumed to have been battle
      trained, as reflected in their price and usage. Because they have
      this training, no extra rolls need be made in a fight, as must be
      made with riding horses.
        Horses that are not combat trained are difficult to handle
      during the press and panic of a bloody fight. In combat riders on
      non-combat trained horses must attempt a Horsemanship roll on
      the Normal Horses in Combat table before any other actions ev-
      ery combat round. Combat-trained horses do not require this roll.
        table 18–1: NorMal Horses iN coMbat
      Horsemanship Effect
      Critical The horse does not need another Horsemanship
              roll for the rest of this fight.
      Success The character may fight as normal.
      Failure The character cannot fight, but can try to evade at-
              tacks with another Horsemanship roll.
      Fumble  No fall is suffered, but the horse broke control
              and bolted out of battle. It runs until another
              Horsemanship roll is made.
      Attack Training

        Horses only begin to be attack-trained in Phase 4.
        An attack trained horse grants a +5 bonus to the user’s
      weapon in melee (not Lance).
        Such a horse is dangerous even out of combat, and normally
      allows only its knight to feed and groom it, even attacking sta-
      ble boys if they come too close. Naturally, such a horse only al-
      lows its own knight to ride it — others who attempt to mount
      provoke a furious attack, which stop only when the miscreant is
      dead, or the knight manages to call off the horse.
      Ruining Horses
        Horses are sturdy, but fragile. Horses can be permanently
      ruined for combat work and hard labor if they are broken. A
      horse is broken if it takes a major wound, or if it fumbles a CON
      roll during a forced march or other extended exertion.
        A broken or old horse of any type is classified as a Nag. Its
      attributes can range widely, but all are unspirited, slow, unin-
      spired, and capable of carrying goods, but nothing else.
        A horse that is broken has its STR and CON each reduced
      by 2, and its Movement Rate reduced by 1.

Extraordinary Horses
     Enchanted or magical horses are extraordinary, but well
  known. Such fine mounts may never be purchased, only gained
  from adventures. Magical horses usually have magical armor or
  movement rates, but other game effects are possible.
     To win an extraordinary horse requires a heroic effort or
  deed, as determined by the Gamemaster. Possibly the trust of
  the steed must be established if it is to accept its position in
  your stable, or mastery be gained through a grueling series of
  Horsemanship rolls, or other efforts.
  faMous Horses

     Bayard: This most famous faerie horse was won by
  Maugis, who gave it to his cousin, Renaud. Bayard is counted
  as a Destrier, with the following changes: He has keen senses
  (Awareness 15), and an almost-human intelligence (he under-
  stands human speech), memory and fidelity. Bayard is fast as the
  wind (Move 25), strong (STR 50), fearless (Valorous 20), very
  dangerous (Vengeful 18) and difficult to tame. He has a sense of
  honor and loyalty (Loyalty [Master] 16). Of Aymon’s four sons,
  Bayard is “the fifth of the four of us.”

     Player-knights may win their own enchanted horse in an

  of their own. They may refuse to flee (Valorous), always wake up
  their master at sunrise, or even stand guard at night (Energetic),

     Dogs are almost as valued as horses. Breeds are unusual, and
  almost all of them are either brachets or gaze hounds. The first
  hunts by scent, the second by sight. A pack of hounds usually
  includes some of each.
     Domesticated dogs are kept in kennels, but are often allowed
  to roam freely during the day. Their role is to guard the domain,
  and to serve during the hunt. Indeed, trained dogs are so useful
  that hunting without a pack of dogs is at –5 to the die rolls.

Animals

        Characters might meet any number of ferocious creatures
      while hunting or on an adventure. The statistics for some of the
      most common, whether domesticated or wild, are given herein.
        Glory Won: This is the amount of Glory gained by slaying
      the creature (if it has attributes as listed; as usual, increase the
      value if the creature’s stats are significantly increased).
        Note the following attributes unique to certain wild crea-
      tures. If any of these attributes is not listed for a particular crea-
      ture, assume that its value is 0.
      Avoidance
        The Avoidance skill, available to beasts and monsters, indi-
      cates how adept the animal is at hiding and escaping from pred-
      ators. Avoidance may occasionally be used for human bandits
      and the like who hide in thick woods, or knights who are crazed.
        During each segment of a hunt, the quarry makes an op-
      posed Avoidance roll against a character’s Hunting skill (or a
      predator’s own Avoidance skill) to evade the hunters.
      Discretion and Valor

        Whenever a character wishes to attack a fierce beast, he
      might be required make a successful Valorous roll upon first
      sighting the creature (what constitutes “fierce” and thus requires
      a roll is left to each Gamemaster’s discretion. In general, magical
      beasts always require a Valorous roll).
        This modifier is a survival factor for young Player-knights
      — creatures too large or too powerful to kill should be avoided
      or placated, not attacked. Thus, a Prudent modifier is also given
      where appropriate; this functions just as the Valorous modifier,
      but with respect to Prudent rolls.
        Failure on a Valorous roll indicates a charac-
      ter’s reluctance to close with the beast for 1 round
      (another roll may be attempted each round),
      while a fumble indicates that the character
      flees in terror for at least 1d6 rounds before
      he returns to his senses. A character who suc-
      ceeds on a Valorous roll but who doesn’t wish
      to attack a particularly fierce creature (such as a
      dragon or giant whom he has no real chance of
      defeating) may then make a Prudent roll to avoid
      the combat, usually without dishonor.
        Note that groups of knights confronting a
      single monster have a better chance of defeating it,
      so any Valorous and Prudent modifiers should
      be divided equally among them. Glory,
      likewise, is divided among the victors.
        Prudent Modifier: This modifier
      applies to any Prudent roll a character
      might make in order to retreat from the
      creature in question without a loss of
      honor; generally, only monsters (and not
      natural beasts) have Prudent modifiers.

  son of Julius Caesar and Morgan le Fay, from whom he inherit-

  a small but extremely beautiful boy, dressed in a white garment
  with golden stripes. He carries an infallible bow (Bow 40) and
  various other powerful enchanted items, which he sometimes
  lends to paladins if they agree to go on certain quests. If so, he
  may act as their spiritual guide.

     Alcina: Morgan’s half-sister. A particularly lustful enchant-
  ress (Lustful 25), very much like Circe of Greek legends. She de-
  lights in capturing heroes within her enchanted castles.
     Falerina: She forged the sword Balisard with the sole aim to
  kill Roland. This vengeful lady (Vengeful 25) resides peacefully in
  the Gardens of Fortune until a paladins sets out on a quest.
     Logistilla: Unlike her half-sisters, Morgan and Alcina,
  Logistilla is a good and helpful faerie, who seeks to promote true
  love (Generous 20, Merciful 15).
     Melissa: This good fay is the guardian of Merlin’s tomb.
  She uses a spellbook to conjure up demons whom she commands
  to do her bidding.
     Oriande: Together with her brother Baudri, this good fa-
  erie raises Maugis at her Castle of Rocheflor.
     Silvanella: Before dying from hopeless love, she enchants
  her tomb to snare passersby into a similar fate (Vengeful 25).
     Faerie Lady (White Lady): White ladies are benign faeries
  living in the Ardennes Forest. They usually have a domestic cow,
  which they let mingle with normal cow herds in the morning,
  but which returns to its faerie home before nightfall. White la-
  dies are generally harmless, and the more benevolent ones may
  even bless new-born babies with good luck, beauty, health, valor,
  strength, honesty, or other such virtues. However, when insult-
  ed, provoked or attacked, they may use their magic abilities like
  faerie enchantresses.
     Half-Faeries: Children born from the union of a hero and
  a faerie enchantress become faeries, not humans. However, hu-
  man children raised by faeries, like Sir Maugis, become half-fa-
  eries, meaning they may learn to use faerie magic. Oliver’s sons
  Aquilon and Grifo are half-faeries; their mother, Gismonda, was
  killed, but they were rescued by good faeries who raised them in
  the land of Faerie, where they grew up to be adult knights in only
  a few years’ time.
  Other  Monsters
     Some unique creatures, found rarely or only in specific loca-
  tions, can be found in Chapter 19: Adventures. If the Gamemaster
  wishes to include them in his game, he should simply make up
  the statistics to suit his desires.
  On a faerie island, Sir Rainouart encounters a terrible cat-
  like monster called Chapalu:
    It had red eyes, Rainouart thought they were aflame;
    Its body was the size of an Aragnonese destrier,
    Its head was horrendous, its face dark,

    It had claws like a leopard and a lion’s tail.
    Observing it, Rainouart signed himself with a cross:
    Never had he been so scared in all of his life.
       — Bataille Loquifer, LXXX
